Here you’ll see dolphins jumping, lovers holding hands, and children playing in the sand… always in pairs. Twin Palms is a beautiful, beach-themed escape from your traditional trick-taking card game. Each round you must manipulate your hand of cards to create unique paired combinations that are stronger (or weaker) than your opponent’s pairs. It's a trick-taker that grants total freedom. No following suit! No trump! But only the cleverest players will hit their bids to earn points. So strategize, and don’t be afraid to change your plans at the last second. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Gameplay 2.1 Deal 2.2 Bid & Bet 2.3 Play Tricks 2.4 Score 3 Player preference options 3.1 Card style 3.2 Font 3.3 Play sound effects Overview Twin Palms is a beautiful escape from your traditional trick-taking card game. A game of Twin Palms is played over several rounds. The number of rounds played depends on the number of players (2/3/4/5 players = 6/6/8/5 rounds). Gameplay Each round will progress through of the following phases in this order: Deal Bid & Bet Play Tricks Score Deal Shuffle the card deck and deal each player a hand of 10 cards. Easy mode uses only 1 suit (Palms), Normal mode uses 2 suits (Palms and Dolphins), and Advanced/Extreme mode use all 3 suits (Palms, Dolphins, Sunglasses). Each suit has 24 cards: 2 copies of 0~10 and wild. Bid & Bet Predict how many tricks you think your cards will win by selecting a Bid card secretly. You may also choose to make a Bet. The amount you can bet is limited by your Bet card options. In 'No bets' mode players cannot place bets. Play Tricks The person with the start player token leads first trick of the round. Players must select exactly two cards from their hand and play them face up. If any of the cards they play are wild, they must announce what number they are assigning to each wild. Wilds can be any number from 0 to 10. Each set of cards played will have a rank defined by the reference card. Whichever player played the highest ranked set of cards wins the trick. Pairs will always beat no pairs. Palms are the strongest, followed by dolphins, followed by Sunglasses, and followed by mixed suits. If two or more players played the same rank, then whoever played the highest numbered card wins. If two or more players play sets of cards with the same rank and numbers (a tie), their cards are discarded and they cannot win the trick. If all players are tied, no one wins the trick and all cards are discarded. The next trick is led out by the previous trick-winner (or the starting player of the round if no one has won a trick yet). Score Once all cards have been played for the round, players score points according to their Bid card and win or lose placed bets. Pass the start player token to the next player and start a new round. Once players have completed the defined number of rounds, the game ends. The player with the most points wins! Player preference options Open upper right menu from game screen or click 'Options' tab below the game board to access these preference options. Card style Original : Uses original card images. Simple: Uses simpler card images with better number visibility. Font Thematic : Uses beach-themed fonts. BGA Default: Uses BGA default fonts. Play sound effects Yes : Plays unique sound effects while dealing or playing cards and scoring. No: Disable sound effects. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] You don’t have to follow suit, but now there’s a tight hierarchy to even understand what you played. And only 5 tricks per hand! For bidding, you get a dozen cards to specify what you even want, and this seems so much more convoluted than anything I’ve ever seen.

[Rating: 2/10] The idea of being able to manipulate the values of your cards mid hand in a trick taker is not new and definitely works with the right parameters (see Whist or Cat in the Box). But those parameters are not here. Unless I am missing something, you can just bid 0 every time, have a larger chance for points, and a way less stressful time during the actual card playing, as it is easier to mess up your own hand on purpose than to predict the number of tricks your hand can take. Strange and sad design, unless I am missing something in the rules or strategy.

[Rating: 3/10] The basic idea of pairing up the cards to make plays is interesting, but with so many cards out of play (at least with three players) and simultaneous bidding it's much too chaotic. Bidding in sequence I think would work better.  ETA: Lowering my rating after trying it with four players. Adding a player didn't help and the game revealed how easy it is to sandbag to make low bids.

[Rating: 3.99/10] One of the worst trick taking games. Pasted on theme (two cards. Hands, palms, palm trees). There's something there but too loose.bga

[Rating: 4/10] A bit convoluted, with playing two cards at a time and having different combinations and suits have different strengths.  Need to play again, but not a top-tier trick-taker.

[Rating: 4/10] The hook is the pairing of cards, but it didn't seem to matter much; the bidding means you can win by just playing your hand at its obvious strength. Maybe you can change your hand's strength by surprising combinations of cards-- didn't seem like it, but I wouldn't know. Because I never had to try!  Anyway, once you get past that you have a functional game but not an interesting one.

[Rating: 4/10] Trick taking with poker pairs. Most of the game is the betting between hands. Overall, this didn't quite grab me the way I thought it would. I wanted something more, some more decision making during the tricks perhaps.

[Rating: 4/10] It is partially broken? Just set the numbers of tricks you will win at 0 and bet the max each round and then intentionally play bad card combinations. Of course if more than one person does this then it becomes difficult but you still have a better chance of hitting your Bid at 0 than any of the higher Bid numbers.  An easy fix which that would add tension and strategy would be to limit the use of each Bid card to one use per GAME and replace one or two of the high bid amounts with another 2 and 3 bid.

[Rating: 4.5/10] Found this to be more of a deduction on reading who will bid what then a trick taker. As zero bid is a little too easy to get, unless everyone bids 0, then it is the first player that has to get rid of of the first trick.

[Rating: 4.7/10] trick taking game  bidding the no of trick to be taken before each round and betting is optional  playing two cards in a turn and wild cards can choose which no simply nothing new in mechanism just with playing pairs

[Rating: 5/10] I like the simple combos and betting so wanted to like this. But the shizawa game ambient abysmal highlights this games deficiencies: the combos are at once too simple yet too complex. Though way more fiddle the game is shallower (since you only go round once and there’s so many of each card).. There are too many of each suit.  And, the theme detracts.
